title: Puncturing for Adaptive Entanglement-Assisted Stabilizer Codes
authors: Nicolai Peder Bülow Pedersen, Jakob Kaltoft Søndergaard, Jaron Skovsted Gundersen, René Bødker Christensen, Petar Popovski
abstract: Quantum error-correcting codes are essential for reliable quantum communication. The achievable parameters can be improved by using entanglement-assisted stabilizers at the cost of consuming pre-shared Bell pairs. If the availability of such Bell pairs is intermittent, the ability to adapt the code to available resources is beneficial. That is, to pick a single mother code that can be adapted to different entanglement budgets. To achieve this, we extend an existing puncturing construction for standard/unassisted stabilizers to the entanglement-assisted setting through a three-step procedure: Interpreting the code as an unassisted stabilizer, puncturing a receiver-side qubit, and recovering an entanglement-assisted representation. This procedure reduces the number of required Bell pairs by one while preserving the number of transmitted and logical qubits. We derive a bound on the resulting distance loss and establish conditions for preserving the original code distance. Finally, we analyse distinct, randomly generated, entanglement-assisted stabilizers with five to eight transmitted qubits. Of these codes, 14.75% have a greater distance than their associated unassisted representations. Among this subset, 81.4% admit at least one puncturing choice that preserves the original entanglement-assisted distance. These results illustrate how puncturing can reduce entanglement requirements while maintaining code distance.
summary: This paper develops a resource-aware puncturing technique for entanglement-assisted quantum error-correcting codes. By adapting existing puncturing methods, the authors show how to reduce the required shared Bell pairs by one while maintaining the code's error-correcting distance. This is vital for building practical quantum communication systems with limited entanglement resources.
main_problem: The paper addresses the need for resource-aware quantum error-correcting codes that can adapt their structure when the availability of pre-shared entanglement (Bell pairs) is intermittent.
main_result: A novel three-step puncturing procedure was developed to extend puncturing constructions from standard stabilizers to entanglement-assisted codes, successfully reducing Bell pair requirements by one while preserving logical qubits and demonstrating distance preservation in most random cases.
method: The method involves interpreting the EAQECC as an unassisted stabilizer, applying a standard puncturing procedure to a receiver-side qubit, and then recovering the entanglement-assisted representation.
model_or_system: The study focuses on Quantum Error-Correcting Codes (QECCs), specifically Entanglement-Assisted Stabilizer Codes (EAQECCs), which use pre-shared Bell pairs to enhance error correction capabilities.
key_observables: Code distance ($d$), number of logical qubits ($k$), number of physical qubits ($n$), and the required number of Bell pairs ($c$).
important_parameters: The fidelity ($F$) of the shared Bell pairs, and the specific structure of the puncturing map applied to the receiver-side qubits.
main_assumptions: The analysis assumes the shared Bell pairs are perfect ($F=1$), and the puncturing procedure is restricted to the receiver's halves of the shared pairs.
figures_summary: Figures illustrate the communication framework for EAQECCs and show histograms analyzing the distance loss ($\Delta_i$) across various puncturing scenarios, confirming distance preservation in a high percentage of cases.
paper_structure: The paper builds from the general theory of stabilizer codes and puncturing, extends this theory to the entanglement-assisted setting via a three-step procedure, derives mathematical bounds on distance loss, and concludes with extensive statistical analysis on randomly generated codes.
why_interesting: This work provides a concrete, systematic method for optimizing quantum resource usage in QEC, which is crucial for scaling up quantum communication protocols that rely on shared entanglement.
